entries.0ab71e32edc4b29c4a98f236991bf53472a89907: <div sID="gen8312" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="2Chr.25" sID="2Chr.25"/> <div eID="gen8312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8313" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8314" type="x-p"/> Amaziah's reign, recorded in this chapter, was not one of the worse and yet for from good. Most of the passages in this chapter we had before more briefly related, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.1-2Kgs.14.22">2 Kings xiv.</reference> Here we find Amaziah, I. A just revenger of his father's death, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.1-2Chr.25.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. An obedient observer of the command of God, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.5-2Chr.25.10">ver. 5-10</reference>. III. A cruel conqueror of the Edomites, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.11-2Chr.25.13">ver. 11-13</reference>. IV. A foolish worshipper of the gods of Edom and impatient of reproof for it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.14-2Chr.25.16">ver. 14-16</reference>. V. Rashly challenging the king of Israel, and smarting for his rashness, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.17-2Chr.25.24">ver. 17-24</reference>. And, lastly, ending his days ingloriously, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.25-2Chr.25.28">ver. 25-28</reference>.
entries.64c3bdfbd89de5358f07ca70b3050dc45309a78d: <div eID="gen8314" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8313" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Amaziah's Reign and Victories. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 838.)</title> <div sID="gen8315" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Amaziah <hi type="italic">was</hi> twenty and five years old <hi type="italic">when</hi> he began to reign, and he reigned twenty and nine years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Jehoaddan of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> right in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , but not with a perfect heart. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now it came to pass, when the kingdom was established to him, that he slew his servants that had killed the king his father. <hi type="super">4</hi> But he slew not their children, but <hi type="italic">did</hi> as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> written in the law in the book of Moses, where the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded, saying, The fathers shall not die for the children, neither shall the children die for the fathers, but every man shall die for his own sin. <hi type="super">5</hi> Moreover Amaziah gathered Judah together, and made them captains over thousands, and captains over hundreds, according to the houses of <hi type="italic">their</hi> fathers, throughout all Judah and Benjamin: and he numbered them from twenty years old and above, and found them three hundred thousand choice <hi type="italic">men, able</hi> to go forth to war, that could handle spear and shield. <hi type="super">6</hi> He hired also a hundred thousand mighty men of valour out of Israel for a hundred talents of silver. <hi type="super">7</hi> But there came a man of God to him, saying, O king, let not the army of Israel go with thee; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> not with Israel, <hi type="italic">to wit, with</hi> all the children of Ephraim. <hi type="super">8</hi> But if thou wilt go, do <hi type="italic">it,</hi> be strong for the battle: God shall make thee fall before the enemy: for God hath power to help, and to cast down. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Amaziah said to the man of God, But what shall we do for the hundred talents which I have given to the army of Israel? And the man of God answered, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> is able to give thee much more than this. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then Amaziah separated them, <hi type="italic">to wit,</hi> the army that was come to him out of Ephraim, to go home again: wherefore their anger was greatly kindled against Judah, and they returned home in great anger. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Amaziah strengthened himself, and led forth his people, and went to the valley of salt, and smote of the children of Seir ten thousand. <hi type="super">12</hi> And <hi type="italic">other</hi> ten thousand <hi type="italic">left</hi> alive did the children of Judah carry away captive, and brought them unto the top of the rock, and cast them down from the top of the rock, that they all were broken in pieces. <hi type="super">13</hi> But the soldiers of the army which Amaziah sent back, that they should not go with him to battle, fell upon the cities of Judah, from Samaria even unto Beth-horon, and smote three thousand of them, and took much spoil. <div eID="gen8315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8316" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The general character of Amaziah: <hi type="italic">He did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord,</hi> worshipped the true God, kept the temple service a going, and countenanced religion in his kingdom; but he did not do it <hi type="italic">with a perfect heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.2">v. 2</reference>), that is, he was not a man of serious piety or devotion himself, nor had he any zeal for the exercises of religion. He was no enemy to it, but a cool and indifferent friend. Such is the character of too many in this Laodicean age: they do that which is good, but not with the heart, not with a perfect heart. <div eID="gen8316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8317" type="x-p"/> II. A necessary piece of justice which he did upon the traitors that murdered his father: he put them to death, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.3">v. 3</reference>. Though we should suppose they intended to avenge on their king the death of the prophet (as was intimated, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.25">ch. xxiv. 25</reference>), yet this would by no means justify their wickedness; for <hi type="italic">they</hi> were not the avengers, but presumptuously took God's work out of his hands: and therefore Amaziah did what became him in calling them to an account for it, but forbade the putting of the children to death for the parents' sin, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.4">v. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen8317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8318" type="x-p"/> III. An expedition of his against the Edomites, who, some time ago, had revolted from under the dominion of Judah, to which he attempted to reduce them. Observe, <div eID="gen8318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8319" type="x-p"/> 1. The great preparation he made for this expedition. (1.) He mustered his own forces, and marshalled them (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.5">v. 5</reference>), and found Judah and Benjamin in all but 300,000 men that were fit for war, whereas, in Jehoshaphat's time, fifty or sixty years before, they were four times as many. Sin weakens a people, diminishes them, dispirits them, and lessens their number and figure. (2.) He hired auxiliary troops out of the kingdom of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.6">v. 6</reference>. Finding his own kingdom defective in men, he thought to make up the deficiency with his money, and therefore took into his pay 100,000 Israelites. If he had advised with any of his prophets before he did this, or had but considered how little any of his ancestors got by their alliances with Israel, he would not have had this to undo again. But rashness makes work for repentance. <div eID="gen8319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8320" type="x-p"/> 2. The command which God sent him by a prophet to dismiss out of his service the forces of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.7-2Chr.25.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. He would not have him call in any assistance at all: it looked like distrust of God. If he made sure of God's presence, the army he had of his own was sufficient. But particularly he must not take in <hi type="italic">their</hi> assistance: <hi type="italic">For the Lord is not with the children of Ephraim, because they are not with him,</hi> but worship the calves. This was a good reason why he should not make use of them, because he could not depend upon them to do him any service. What good could be expected from those that had not God with them, nor his blessings upon their undertakings? It is comfortable to employ those who, we have reason to hope, have an interest in heaven, and dangerous to associate with those from whom the Lord has departed. The prophet assured him that if he persisted in his resolution to take these idolatrous apostate Israelites with him, in hopes thereby to make himself strong for the battle, it was at his peril; they would prove a dead weight to his army, would sink and betray it: "<hi type="italic">God shall make thee fall before the enemy,</hi> and these Israelites will be the ruin of thy cause; for God has power to help thee without them, and to cast thee down though thou hast them with thee." <div eID="gen8320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8321" type="x-p"/> 3. The objection which Amaziah made against this command, and the satisfactory answer which the prophet gave to that objection, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.9">v. 9</reference>. The king had remitted 100 talents to the men of Israel for advance-money. "Now," says he, "if I send them back, I shall lose that: <hi type="italic">But what shall we do for the 100 talents?</hi>" This is an objection men often make against their duty: they are afraid of losing by it. "Regard not that," says the prophet: "<hi type="italic">The Lord is able to give thee much more than this;</hi> and, thou mayest depend upon it, he will not see thee lose by him. What are 100 talents between thee and him? He has ways enough to make up the loss to thee; it is below thee to speak of it." Note, A firm belief of God's all-sufficiency to bear us out in our duty, and to make up all the loss and damage we sustain in his service abundantly to our advantage, will make his yoke very easy and his burden very light. What is it to trust in God, but to be willing to venture the loss of any thing for him, in confidence of the goodness of the security he gives us that we shall not lose by him, but that whatever we part with for his sake shall be made up to us in kind or kindness. When we grudge to part with any thing for God and our religion, this should satisfy us, that God is able to give us much more than this. He is just, and he is good, and he is solvent. The king lost 100 talents by his obedience; and we find just that sum given to his grandson Jotham as a present (<reference osisRef="2Chr.27.5">ch. xxvii. 5</reference>); then the principal was repaid, and, for interest, 10,000 measures of wheat and as many of barley. <div eID="gen8321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8322" type="x-p"/> 4. His obedience to the command of God, which is upon record to his honour. He would rather lose his money, disoblige his allies, and dismiss a fourth part of his army just as they were going to take the field, than offend God: <hi type="italic">He separated the army of Ephraim, to go home again,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.10">v. 10</reference>. And they went home in great anger, taking it as a great affront thus to be made fools of, and to be cashiered as men not fit to be employed, and being perhaps disappointed of the advantages they promised themselves in spoil and plunder by joining with Judah against Edom. Men are apt to resent that which touches them in their profit or reputation, though it frees them from trouble. <div eID="gen8322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8323" type="x-p"/> 5. His triumphs over the Edomites, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.11-2Chr.25.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. He left dead upon the spot, in the field of battle, 10,000 men; 10,000 more he took prisoners, and barbarously killed them all by throwing them down some steep and craggy precipice. What provocation he had to exercise this cruelty towards them we are not told; but it was certainly very severe. <div eID="gen8323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8324" type="x-p"/> 6. The mischief which the disbanded soldiers of Israel did to the cities of Judah, either in their return or soon after, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.13">v. 13</reference>. They were so enraged at being sent home that, if they might not go to share with Judah in the spoil of Edom, they would make a prey of Judah. Several cities that lay upon the borders they plundered, killing 3000 men that made resistance. But why should God suffer this to be done? Was it not in obedience to him that they were sent home, and yet shall the country thus suffer by it? Surely God's way is in the sea! Did not the prophet say that God was not with the children of Ephraim, and yet they are suffered to prevail against Judah? Doubtless God intended hereby to chastise those cities of Judah for their idolatries, which were found most in those parts that lay next to Israel. The men of Israel had corrupted them, and now they were made a plague to them. Satan both tempts and torments.
entries.c5dbf337b598053bb79a132341ccd2826e9c271d: <div eID="gen8324" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Amaziah's Idolatry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 826.)</title> <div sID="gen8325" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Now it came to pass, after that Amaziah was come from the slaughter of the Edomites, that he brought the gods of the children of Seir, and set them up <hi type="italic">to be</hi> his gods, and bowed down himself before them, and burned incense unto them. <hi type="super">15</hi> Wherefore the anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was kindled against Amaziah, and he sent unto him a prophet, which said unto him, Why hast thou sought after the gods of the people, which could not deliver their own people out of thine hand? <hi type="super">16</hi> And it came to pass, as he talked with him, that <hi type="italic">the king</hi> said unto him, Art thou made of the king's counsel? forbear; why shouldest thou be smitten? Then the prophet forbare, and said, I know that God hath determined to destroy thee, because thou hast done this, and hast not hearkened unto my counsel. <div eID="gen8325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8326" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The revolt of Amaziah from the God of Israel to the gods of the Edomites. Egregious folly! Ahaz worshipped the gods of those that had conquered him, for which he had some little colour, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.23">ch. xxviii. 23</reference>. But to worship the gods of those whom he had conquered, who could not protect their own worshippers, was the greatest absurdity that could be. What did he see in the gods of the children of Seir that could tempt him to set them up for <hi type="italic">his gods</hi> and <hi type="italic">bow himself down before them?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.14">v. 14</reference>. If he had cast the idols down from the rock and broken them to pieces, instead of the prisoners, he would have manifested more of the piety as well as more of the pity of an Israelite; but perhaps for that barbarous inhumanity he was given up to this ridiculous idolatry. <div eID="gen8326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8327" type="x-p"/> II. The reproof which God sent to him, by a prophet, for this sin. <hi type="italic">The anger of the Lord was kindled against him,</hi> and justly; yet, before he sent to destroy him, he sent to convince and reclaim him, and so to prevent his destruction. The prophet reasoned with him very fairly and very mildly: <hi type="italic">Why hast thou sought</hi> the favour of those gods <hi type="italic">which could not deliver their own people?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.15">v. 15</reference>. If men would but duly consider the inability of all those things to help them to which they have recourse when they forsake God, they would not be such enemies to themselves. <div eID="gen8327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8328" type="x-p"/> III. The check he gave to the reprover, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.16">v. 16</reference>. He could say nothing in excuse of his own folly; the reproof was too just to be answered. But he fell into a passion with the reprover. 1. He taunted him as saucy and impertinent, and meddling with that which did not belong to him: <hi type="italic">Art thou made of the king's counsel?</hi> Could not a man speak reasonably to him, but he must be upbraided as usurping the place of a privy-counsellor? But, as a prophet, he really was made of the king's counsel by the King of kings, in duty to whom the king was bound not only to hear, but to ask and take his counsel. 2. He silenced him, bade him forbear and say not a word more to him. He <hi type="italic">said to the seer, See not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Isa. xxx. 10</reference>. Men would gladly have their prophets thus under their girdles, as we say, to speak just when and what they would have them speak, and not otherwise. 3. He threatened him: "<hi type="italic">Why shouldst thou be smitten?</hi> It is at thy peril if thou sayest a word more of this matter." He seems to remind him of Zechariah's fate in the last reign, who was put to death for making bold with the king; and bids him take warning by him. Thus he justifies the killing of that prophet by menacing this, and so, in effect, makes himself guilty of the blood of both. He had hearkened to the prophet who ordered him to send back the army of Israel, and was ruled by him, though he contradicted his politics and lost him 100 talents, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.10">v. 10</reference>. But this prophet, who dissuaded him from worshipping the gods of the Edomites, he ran upon with an unaccountable rage, which must be attributed to the witchcraft of idolatry. He was easily persuaded to part with his talents of silver, but by no means with his gods of silver. <div eID="gen8328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8329" type="x-p"/> IV. The doom which the prophet passed upon him for this. He had more to say to him by way of instruction and advice; but, finding him obstinate in his iniquity, he forbore. He is <hi type="italic">joined to idols; let him alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.4.17">Hos. iv. 17</reference>. Miserable is the condition of that man with whom the blessed Spirit, by ministers and conscience, <hi type="italic">forbears to strive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen. vi. 3</reference>. And both the reprovers in the gate and that in the bosom, if long brow-beaten and baffled, will at length forbear. So I <hi type="italic">gave them up to their own hearts' lusts.</hi> The secure sinner perhaps values himself upon it as a noble and happy achievement to have silenced his reprovers and monitors, and to get clear of them; but what comes of it? "<hi type="italic">I know that God has determined to destroy thee;</hi> it is a plain indication that thou art marked for ruin <hi type="italic">that thou hast done this, and hast not hearkened to my counsel.</hi>" Those that are deaf to reproof are ripening apace for destruction, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.1">Prov. xxix. 1</reference>.
entries.381f4517d6e5cd49304603ca340221448ab9ceef: <div eID="gen8329" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Death of Amaziah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 825.)</title> <div sID="gen8330" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Then Amaziah king of Judah took advice, and sent to Joash, the son of Jehoahaz, the son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, Come, let us see one another in the face. <hi type="super">18</hi> And Joash king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, The thistle that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Lebanon sent to the cedar that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Lebanon, saying, Give thy daughter to my son to wife: and there passed by a wild beast that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Lebanon, and trode down the thistle. <hi type="super">19</hi> Thou sayest, Lo, thou hast smitten the Edomites; and thine heart lifteth thee up to boast: abide now at home; why shouldest thou meddle to <hi type="italic">thine</hi> hurt, that thou shouldest fall, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thou, and Judah with thee? <hi type="super">20</hi> But Amaziah would not hear; for it <hi type="italic">came</hi> of God, that he might deliver them into the hand <hi type="italic">of their enemies,</hi> because they sought after the gods of Edom. <hi type="super">21</hi> So Joash the king of Israel went up; and they saw one another in the face, <hi type="italic">both</hi> he and Amaziah king of Judah, at Beth-shemesh, which <hi type="italic">belongeth</hi> to Judah. <hi type="super">22</hi> And Judah was put to the worse before Israel, and they fled every man to his tent. <hi type="super">23</hi> And Joash the king of Israel took Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Joash, the son of Jehoahaz, at Beth-shemesh, and brought him to Jerusalem, and brake down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, four hundred cubits. <hi type="super">24</hi> And <hi type="italic">he took</hi> all the gold and the silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God with Obed-edom, and the treasures of the king's house, the hostages also, and returned to Samaria. <hi type="super">25</hi> And Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah lived after the death of Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel fifteen years. <hi type="super">26</hi> Now the rest of the acts of Amaziah, first and last, behold, <hi type="italic">are</hi> they not written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel? <hi type="super">27</hi> Now after the time that Amaziah did turn away from following the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem; and he fled to Lachish: but they sent to Lachish after him, and slew him there. <hi type="super">28</hi> And they brought him upon horses, and buried him with his fathers in the city of Judah. <div eID="gen8330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8331" type="x-p"/> We have here this degenerate prince mortified by his neighbour and murdered by his own subjects. <div eID="gen8331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8332" type="x-p"/> I. Never was proud prince more thoroughly mortified than Amaziah was by Joash king of Israel. <div eID="gen8332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8333" type="x-p"/> 1. This part of the story (which was as fully related <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.8-2Kgs.14.22">2 Kings xiv. 8</reference>, &c., as it is here)—embracing the foolish challenge which Amaziah sent to Joash (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.17">v. 17</reference>), his haughty scornful answer to it (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.18">v. 18</reference>), with the friendly advice he gave him to sit still and know when he was well off, (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.19">v. 19</reference>),—his wilfully persisting in his challenge (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.20-2Chr.25.21">v. 20, 21</reference>), the defeat that was given him (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.22">v. 22</reference>), and the calamity he brought upon himself and his city thereby (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.23-2Chr.25.24">v. 23, 24</reference>),—verifies two of Solomon's proverbs:—(1.) That <hi type="italic">a man's pride will bring him low,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.23">Prov. xxix. 23</reference>. It goes before his destruction; not only procures it meritoriously, but is often the immediate occasion of it. <hi type="italic">He that exalteth himself shall be abased.</hi> (2.) That he that <hi type="italic">goes forth hastily to strive</hi> will probably not know what to do in the end thereof, <hi type="italic">when his neighbour has put him to shame,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.8">Prov. xxv. 8</reference>. He that is fond of contention may have enough of it sooner than he thinks of. <div eID="gen8333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8334" type="x-p"/> 2. But there are two passages in this story which we had not before in the <hi type="italic">Kings.</hi> (1.) That <hi type="italic">Amaziah took advice</hi> before he challenged the king of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.17">v. 17</reference>. But of whom? Not of the prophet—he was <hi type="italic">not made of the king's counsel;</hi> but of his statesmen that would flatter him and bid him go up and prosper. It is good to take advice, but then it must be of those that are fit to advise us. Those that will not take advice from the word of God, which would guide them aright, will justly be left to the bad advice of those that will counsel them to their destruction. Let those be made fools that will not be made wise. (2.) Amaziah's imprudence is here made the punishment of his impiety (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">It was of the Lord;</hi> he left him to himself to act thus foolishly, that he and his people might be <hi type="italic">delivered into the hands of their enemies, because</hi> they had forsaken God and <hi type="italic">sought after the gods of Edom.</hi> Those that will not persuaded to do well for their souls will justly be given up to their own counsels to do ill for themselves even in their outward affairs. <div eID="gen8334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8335" type="x-p"/> II. Never was poor prince more violently pursued by his own subjects. <hi type="italic">From the time</hi> that he departed from the Lord (so it may be read, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.27">v. 27</reference>) the hearts of his subjects departed from him, and they began to form a design against him in Jerusalem. It is probable they were exasperated against him more for his rashly engaging in a war against Israel than for his worshipping the gods of Edom. But at length the ferment grew so high, and he perceived the plot to be laid so deeply, that he thought fit to quit his royal city and flee to Lachish, either as a private place where he might be hid or as a strong place where he might be guarded; but they sent after him thither, and slew him there. By this the putting of him to death seems to have been done deliberately, and to have been the act, not of a disgusted servant or two, but of a considerable body that durst avow it. How unrighteous soever they were herein, God was righteous.  <chapter eID="2Chr.25"/> <div eID="gen8335" type="x-p"/>

entries.b4ad63e246a2bf0446dba9c2b3cdf27fac63c3e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4094"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 25</title> <div sID="gen5932" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.1-2Chr.25.4">2Ch 25:1-4</reference>. Amaziah Begins to Reign Well.<div eID="gen5932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5933" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4094"/><hi type="bold">1. Amaziah was twenty and five years old, &c.--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.1-2Kgs.14.6">2Ki 14:1-6</reference>).<div eID="gen5933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5934" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.5-2Chr.25.10">2Ch 25:5-10</reference>. Having Hired an Army of Israelites against the Edomites, at the Word of a Prophet He Loses a Hundred Talents and Dismisses Them. <div eID="gen5934" type="x-p"/>
entries.0fa572cece02ddd26840f75073f6047ab5eb2f45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4095"/><div sID="gen5935" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4095"/><hi type="bold">5. Amaziah ... made captains, &c.--</hi>As all who were capable of bearing arms were liable to serve, it was quite natural in making up the muster-roll to class them according to their respective families and to appoint the officers of each corps from the same quarter; so that all the soldiers who formed a regiment were brothers, relatives, friends. Thus the Hebrew troops were closely linked together, and had strong inducements to keep steady in their ranks.<div eID="gen5935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">found them three hundred thousand choice men--</hi>This was only a fourth part of Jehoshaphat's army (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.14-2Chr.17.19">2Ch 17:14-19</reference>), showing how sadly the kingdom of Judah had, in the space of eighty-two years, been reduced in population by foreign wars, no less than by internal corruptions. But the full amount of Amaziah's troops may not be here stated. <div eID="gen5936" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe7b1ffc15fe053a20749ff8f3733f960eaa661f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4096"/><div sID="gen5937" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4096"/><hi type="bold">6. He hired also an hundred thousand mighty men of valour ... for an hundred talents of silver--</hi>This sum was paid into the treasury of Jehoahaz--not given as bounty to the mercenaries who were obliged to serve at the sovereign's call; their remuneration consisting only in the booty they might obtain. It was about £50,000 sterling, being 10s. per man, including officers--a very paltry pay, compared with the bounty given for a soldier in this country. But it must be remembered that in ancient times campaigns were short and the hazards of the service comparatively small. <div eID="gen5937" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a3ba8f30184482d2407cbc47180399ca7e44539: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4097"/><div sID="gen5938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4097"/><hi type="bold">7-8. there came a man of God--</hi>sent to dissuade Amaziah from the course he was following, on the ground that "the Lord is not with Israel." This statement was perfectly intelligible to the king. But the historian, writing long after, thought it might require explanation, and therefore added the comment, "with all the children of Ephraim." Idolatry had long been the prevailing religion in that kingdom, and Ephraim its headquarters. As to the other part of the prophet's advice (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.8">2Ch 25:8</reference>), considerable obscurity hangs over it, as the text stands; and hence some able critics have suggested the insertion of "not" in the middle clause, so that the verse will be thus: "But if thou wilt go [alone], do, be strong for the battle; God shall not make thee fall before the enemy." <div eID="gen5938" type="x-p"/>
entries.3bb5140791675e9551e6ed17f7dbac4aeb3f0f9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4098"/><div sID="gen5939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4098"/><hi type="bold">10. separated them ... the army ... out of Ephraim ... their anger was greatly kindled against Judah--</hi>Amaziah, who knew his position as the Lord's viceroy, complied with the prophet's counsel, and, consenting to forfeit the purchase money of the Israelitish soldiers, discharged them. Exasperated at this treatment, they resolved to indemnify themselves for the loss of their expected booty, and so on their return home they plundered all the towns in their way, committing great havoc both of life and property without any stoppage, as the king of Judah and his army had set out on their expedition (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.7">2Ki 14:7</reference>). <div eID="gen5939" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8977b9c5334db30f1a131f8b53597cf908907c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4099"/><div sID="gen5940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4099"/><hi type="bold">11. valley of salt--</hi>This ravine lies to the south of the Dead Sea. The arms of Amaziah, in reward for his obedience to the divine will, were crowned with victory--ten thousand of the Edomites were slain on the field, and as many taken prisoners, who were put to death by precipitation "from the top of the rock" [2Ch 25:12]. This rock might be situated in the neighborhood of the battlefield, but more probably it formed one of the high craggy cliffs of Selah (Petra), the capital of the Edomites, whither Amaziah marched directly from the Valley of Salt, and which he captured (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.7">2Ki 14:7</reference>). The savage cruelty dealt out to them was either in retaliation for similar barbarities inflicted on the Hebrews, or to strike terror into so rebellious a people for the future. The mode of execution, by dashing against stones (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.9">Psa 137:9</reference>), was common among many ancient nations. <div eID="gen5940" type="x-p"/>
entries.276ccf88f8b0c6b6253ceef6d5f633ebce4ec1db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4100"/><div sID="gen5941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4100"/><hi type="bold">14-16. Amaziah ... brought the gods of the children of Seir--</hi>The Edomites worshipped the sun under different forms and with various rites. But burning incense upon altars was a principal act of worship, and this was the very thing Amaziah is described as having with strange infatuation performed. Whether he had been captivated with the beauty of the images, or hoped by honoring the gods to disarm their spite at him for his conquest and harsh treatment of their votaries, his conduct in establishing these objects of religious homage in Jerusalem was foolish, ignorant, and highly offensive to God, who commissioned a prophet to rebuke him for his apostasy, and threaten him with the calamity that soon after befell him. <div eID="gen5941" type="x-p"/>
entries.3632ff7289e516efc04f9473bd2b42b12646b23e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4102"/><div sID="gen5944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4102"/><hi type="bold">17. Then Amaziah ... sent to Joash ... Come, let us see one another in the face--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.8-2Kgs.14.20">2Ki 14:8-20</reference>). <chapter eID="2Chr.25"/>

entries.44b9cc995f967d1aa3eb47091e666b663bbc641b: <div eID="gen14453" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14454" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14455" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14455" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14454" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14456" type="x-p"/> Amaziah succeeds his father Joash, and begins his reign well, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.1">2Chr 25:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.2">2Chr 25:2</reference>. He slays his father's murderers but spares their children, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.3">2Chr 25:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.4">2Chr 25:4</reference>. He reviews and remodels the army, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.5">2Chr 25:5</reference>; and hires a hundred thousand soldiers out of Israel, whom, on the expostulation of a prophet, he sends home again, without bringing them into active service; at which they are greatly offended, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.6-2Chr.25.10">2Chr 25:6-10</reference>. He attacks the Syrians, kills ten thousand, and takes ten thousand prisoners, whom he precipitates from the top of a rock, so that they are dashed to pieces, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.11">2Chr 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.12">2Chr 25:12</reference>. The Israelitish soldiers, sent back, ravage several of the cities of Judah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.13">2Chr 25:13</reference>. Amaziah becomes an idolater, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.14">2Chr 25:14</reference>. Is reproved by a prophet, whom he threatens, and obliges to desist, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.15">2Chr 25:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.16">2Chr 25:16</reference>. He challenges Joash, king of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.17">2Chr 25:17</reference>; who reproves him by a parable, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.18">2Chr 25:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.19">2Chr 25:19</reference>. Not desisting, the armies meet, the Jews are overthrown, and Amaziah taken prisoner by Joash, who ravages the temple, and takes away all the treasures of the king, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.20-2Chr.25.24">2Chr 25:20-24</reference>. The reign of Amaziah: a conspiracy is formed against him; he flees to Lachish, whither he is pursued and slain; is brought to Jerusalem, and buried with his fathers, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.25-2Chr.25.28">2Chr 25:25-28</reference>.
entries.6b732cc13425ac9ad95f0ba3308b1ccb11023259: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen14456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14457" type="x-p"/> He did that which was right - He began his reign well, but soon became an idolater, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.14">2Chr 25:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.15">2Chr 25:15</reference>.
entries.40a4100ec9cfd21845cabd89c59495091dc3a5c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen14457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14458" type="x-p"/> Gathered Judah together - He purposed to avenge himself of the Syrians, but wished to know his military strength before he came to a rupture.
entries.51dd6ea1c6bf57b00e21ac3fb7dedc701096ea6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen14458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14459" type="x-p"/> The Lord is not with Israel - "The Word of the Lord is not the helper of the Israelites, nor of the kingdom of the tribe of Ephraim." - Targum.
entries.31e94210941f49d438fe90b2b24179312fcbc5a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14460" type="x-p"/> The Lord is able to give thee much more than this - Better lose the money than keep the men, for they will be a curse unto thee.
entries.fb46f02ee2e9aa1dd26af74a687948ffe9daf8d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen14460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14461" type="x-p"/> They returned home in great anger - They thought they were insulted, and began to meditate revenge. See the notes on 2 Kings 14:1-20 (note), where almost every circumstance in this chapter is examined and explained.
entries.10776394f1ce9ae4ca5dc24a99ce426451337a55: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen14461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14462" type="x-p"/> The gods of the children of Seir - "The idols of the children of Gebal." - Targum.
entries.5ff0f3d4a2b4c7d5e154ef0beefe70b78005b3d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen14462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14463" type="x-p"/> Art thou made of the king's counsel? - How darest thou give advice to, or reprove, a king?
entries.97e21728a6039070c1ea5ed81d9dd34c429b5e6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen14463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14464" type="x-p"/> The thistle that was in Lebanon - See the explanation of this <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.9">2Kgs 14:9</reference> (note). After reciting this fable, the Targum adds, "Thus hast thou done in the time thou didst send unto me, and didst lead up from the house of Israel a hundred thousand strong warriors for a hundred talents of silver: and after they were sent, thou didst not permit them to go with thee to war, but didst send them back, greatly enraged, so that they spread themselves over the country; and having cut off three thousand, they brought back much spoil."
entries.46d8256e8c3273b2e73c36439a187b50854e556b: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen14464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14465" type="x-p"/> In the house of God with Obed-edom - From <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.15">1Chr 26:15</reference> we learn that to Obed-edom and his descendants was allotted the keeping of the house of Asuppim or collections for the Divine treasury. <div eID="gen14465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14466" type="x-p"/> And - the hostages - See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.14">2Kgs 14:14</reference> (note).
entries.c34a70ee88922051632ec22ddde828d2e0dc2158: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen14466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14467" type="x-p"/> The rest of the acts of Amaziah, first and last - Says the Targum; "The first, when he walked in the fear of the Lord, the last, when he departed from the right way before the Lord; are they not written," etc.
entries.6ffa41b674c0849ac19b8cde613d1a4a793bc77a: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen14467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14468" type="x-p"/> Made a conspiracy - He no doubt became very unpopular after having lost the battle with the Israelites; the consequence of which was the dismantling of Jerusalem, and the seizure of the royal treasures, with several other evils. It is likely that the last fifteen years of his reign were greatly embittered: so that, finding the royal city to be no place of safety, he endeavored to secure himself at Lachish; but all in vain, for thither his murderers pursued him; and he who forsook the Lord was forsaken by every friend, perished in his gainsaying, and came to an untimely end.  <chapter eID="2Chr.25"/> <div eID="gen14468" type="x-p"/>

entries.c973dc78e4d508fea08485f89e58870f0dda9b34: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.1-2Chr.25.4">2Ch 25:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen6106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6107" type="x-p"/> The statement as to the duration and spirit of the reign agrees with 2Ki 14:1-6, except that in <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.2">2Ch 25:2</reference> the estimation of the spirit of the reign according to the standard of David, “only not as his ancestor David, but altogether as his father Joash did,” which we find in the book of Kings, is replaced by “only not with a perfect heart;” and the standing formula, “only the high places were not removed,” etc., is omitted. <div eID="gen6107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6108" type="x-p"/> The succeeding section, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.5-2Chr.25.16">2Ch 25:5-16</reference>, enlarges upon Amaziah’s preparations for war with Edom, which had revolted under Joram of Judah, 2Ki 8:22; upon the victory over the Edomites in the Valley of Salt, and on the results of this war; - on all which we have in 2Ki 14:7 only this short note: “he smote Edom in the valley of Salt 10,000 men, and took Selah in war, and called its name Joktheel unto this day.” But the more exact statements of the Chronicle as to the preparations and the results of this war and victory are important for Amaziah’s later war with Kings Joash of Israel, which is narrated in 2Ch 25:17. of our chapter, because in them lie the causes of that war, so fatal to Amaziah; so that the history of Amaziah is essentially supplemented by those statements of the Chronicle which are not found in 2 Kings.
entries.f053f661869e5481b55ec545bda737027c98c790: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.5-2Chr.25.7">2Ch 25:5-7</reference> <hi type="italic">The preparations for the war against Edom, and the victory over the Edomites in the Valley of Salt</hi>. - 2Ch 25:5. Amaziah assembled Judah, i.e., the men in his kingdom capable of bearing arms, and set them up (ordered them) according to the princes of thousands and hundreds, of all Judah and Benjamin, and passed them in review, i.e., caused a census to be taken of the men liable to military service from twenty years old and upward. They found 300,000 warriors “bearing spear and target” (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.7">2Ch 14:7</reference>); a relatively small number, not merely in comparison with the numbers under Jehoshaphat, 2Ch 17:14., which are manifestly too large, but also with the numberings made by other kings, e.g., Asa, 2Ch 14:7. By Joram’s unfortunate wars, <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.17">2Ch 21:17</reference>, those of Ahaziah, and especially by the defeat which Joash sustained from the Syrians, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.23">2Ch 24:23</reference>, the number of men in Judah fit for war may have been very much reduced. Amaziah accordingly sought to strengthen his army against the Edomites, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.6">2Ch 25:6</reference>, by having an auxiliary corps of 100,000 men from Israel (of the ten tribes) for 100 talents of silver, i.e., he took them into his pay. But a prophet advised him not to take the Israelitish host with him, because Jahve was not with Israel, viz., on account of their defection from Jahve by the introduction of the calf-worship. To Israel there is added, (with) all the sons of Ephraim, to guard against any misunderstanding.
entries.e972e4f71320f7c75bd03de913b8f7a9d0e050d2: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.8">2Ch 25:8</reference> <div eID="gen6108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6109" type="x-p"/> Amaziah is to go alone, and show himself valiant in war, and the Lord will help him to conquer. This is without doubt the thought in <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.8">2Ch 25:8</reference>, which, however, does not seem to be contained in the traditional Masoretic text. האל יכשׁילך can hardly, after the preceding imperatives - do, be strong for battle - be otherwise translated than by, “and God will cause thee to stumble before the enemy.” But this is quite unsuitable. Clericus, therefore, would take the words ironically: <hi type="italic">sin minus, tu vadito,</hi> etc.; i.e., if thou dost not follow my advice, and takest the Israelites with thee to the war, go, show thyself strong for the war, God will soon cause thee to stumble. But אם כּי can never signify <hi type="italic">sin minus</hi>. Others, as Schmidt and Ramb., translate: Rather do thou go alone (without the Israelitish auxiliaries), and be valiant, <hi type="italic">alioquin enim, si illos tecum duxeris, corruere te faciet Deus;</hi> or, May God make thee fall before the enemy (De Wette). But the supplying of <hi type="italic">alioquin</hi>, which is only hidden by De Wette’s translation, cannot be grammatically justified. This interpretation of the יכשׁילך would be possible only if the negation לא אם כּי stood in the preceding clause and יכשׁילך was joined to it by ו. The traditional text is clearly erroneous, and we must, with Ewald and Berth., supply a לא or ולא before יכשׁילך: God thou (alone), do, be valiant for battle, and God will not let thee come to ruin.<note placement="foot">Even the old translators could make nothing of the present text, and expressed the first clause of the verse as they thought best. lxx, ὅτι ἐὰν ὑπολάβης κατασχῦσαι ἐν τούτοις; Vulg., <hi type="italic">quod si putes in robore exercitus bella consistere;</hi> after which Luth., “<hi type="italic">denn so du komest das du eine künheit beweisest im streit, wird Gott dich fallen lassen für deinen Feinden</hi>.”</note> <div eID="gen6109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6110" type="x-p"/> After this we have very fittingly the reason assigned: “for with God there is power to help, and to cause to fall.”
entries.39470bedf9b78606e4d9d14bef4caa48600dbf64: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.9-2Chr.25.10">2Ch 25:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen6110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6111" type="x-p"/> Amaziah had regard to this exhortation of the prophet, and asked him only what he should do for the 100 talents of silver which he had paid the Israelite auxiliary corps; to which the prophet answered that Jahve could give him more than that sum. Amaziah thereupon dismissed the hired Ephraimite mercenaries. יבדּילם, he separated them (sc., from his army prepared for battle), viz., the band, that they might go to their place, i.e., might return home. The ל before הגּדוּד is <hi type="italic">nota accus</hi>., and להגּדוּד is in apposition to the suffix in יבדּילם. But the auxiliaries thus dismissed returned home full of wrath against Judah, and afterwards fell upon the border cities of Judah, wasting and plundering (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.13">2Ch 25:13</reference>). Their anger probably arose from the fact that by their dismissal the opportunity of making a rich booty in war was taken away.
entries.d0d7100e84021cbc2af2246c247ff1aed4a6aaa4: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.11-2Chr.25.12">2Ch 25:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen6111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6112" type="x-p"/> But Amaziah courageously led his people into the Valley of Salt, and smote the Edomites. התחזק, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8">2Ch 15:8</reference>, refers back to חזק, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.8">2Ch 25:8</reference> : he showed himself strong, according to the word of the prophet. As to the Valley of Salt, see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.13">2Sa 8:13</reference> and 1Ch 18:12. Besides the 10,000 slain in the battle, the men of Judah took 10,000 other Edomites prisoners, whom they cast from the top of a rock. This statement is wanting in 2Ki 14:7, where, instead of it, the capture of the city Sela (Petra) is mentioned. The conjecture of Thenius, that this last statement of the Chronicle has been derived from a text of the Kings which had become illegible at this place, has already been rejected as untenable by Bertheau. Except the word סלע, the two texts have nothing in common with each other; but it does suggest itself that הסּלע ראשׁ, the top of the rock (which has become famous by this event), is to be looked for in the neighbourhood of the city Selah, as the war was ended only by the capture of Selah. Besides the battle in the Valley of Salt there were still further battles; and in the numbers 10,000, manifestly the whole of the prisoners taken in the war are comprehended, who, as irreconcilable enemies of Judah, were not made slaves, but were slain by being thrown down from a perpendicular rock.
entries.a19e79dc5396b3ba0e099e4142ff9747e7a53938: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.13">2Ch 25:13</reference> <div eID="gen6112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6113" type="x-p"/> The Ephraimite host dismissed by Amaziah fell plundering upon the cities of Judah, and smote of them (the inhabitants of these cities) 3000, and carried away great booty. They would seem to have made this devastating attack on their way home; but to this idea, which at first suggests itself, the more definite designation of the plundered cities, “from Samaria to Bethhoron,” does not correspond, for these words can scarcely be otherwise understood than as denoting that Samaria was the starting-point of the foray, and not the limit up to which the plundered cities reached. For this reason Berth. thinks that this attack upon the northern cities of Judah was probably carried out only at a later period, when Amaziah and his army were in Edom. The latter is certainly the more probable supposition; but the course of events can hardly have been, that the Ephraimite auxiliary corps, after Amaziah had dismissed it, returned home to Samaria, and then later, when Amaziah had marched into the Valley of Salt, made this attack upon the cities of Judah, starting from Samaria. It is more probable that the dismissal of this auxiliary corps, which Amaziah had certainly obtained on hire from King Joash, happened after they had been gathered together in Samaria, and had advanced to the frontier of Judah. Then, roused to anger by their dismissal, they did not at once separate and return home; but, Amaziah having meanwhile taken the field against the Edomites with his army, made an attack upon the northern frontier cities of Judah as far as Bethhoron, plundering as they went, and only after this plundering did they return home. As to Bethhoron, now Beit-Ur, see on 1Ch 7:24.
entries.fd65cca55713fbabe923dc218386a2a0a16caba4: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.14-2Chr.25.15">2Ch 25:14-15</reference> <hi type="italic">Amaziah’s idolatry</hi>. - 2Ch 25:14. On his return from smiting the Edomites, i.e., from the war in which he had smitten the Edomites, Amaziah brought the gods (images) of the sons of Seir (the inhabitants of Mount Seir) with him, and set them up as gods, giving them religious adoration.<note placement="foot">This statement, which is not found in 2 Kings 14, may, in the opinion of Berth., perhaps not rest upon a definite tradition, but be merely the application of a principle which generally was found to act in the history of Israel to a particular case; i.e., it may be a clothing in historical garments of the principle that divine punishment came upon the idolatrous king, because it does not agree with the statement of 2Ki 14:3. In that passage it is said of Amaziah: He did what was right in the eyes of Jahve, only not as David; altogether as his father Joash had done, did he. But Joash allowed his princes, after Jehoiada’s death, to worship idols and Asheras, and had caused the prophet Zechariah, who reproved this idolatry, to be stoned. These are facts which, it is true, are narrated only in the Chronicle, but which are admitted by Bertheau himself to be historical. Now if Amaziah did altogether the same as his father Joash, who allowed idolatry, etc., it is hard indeed to see wherein the inconsistency of our account of Amaziah’s idolatry with the character assigned to this king in 2Ki 14:3 consists. Bertheau has omitted to give us any more definite information on this point.</note> <div eID="gen6113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6114" type="x-p"/> In order to turn him away from this sin, which would certainly kindle Jahve’s wrath, a prophet said to Amaziah, “Why dost thou seek the gods of the people, who have not delivered their people out of your hand?” The prophet keeps in view the motive which had induced the king to set up and worship the Edomite idols, viz., the belief of all polytheists, that in order to make a people subject, one must seek to win over their gods (cf. on this belief that remarks on Num 22:17), and exposes the folly of this belief by pointing out the impotence of the Edomite idols, which Amaziah himself had learnt to know.
entries.58b6ba31db03a7bc7716232f06335da45a68fa74: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.16">2Ch 25:16</reference> <div eID="gen6114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6115" type="x-p"/> The king, however, in his blindness puts aside this earnest warning with proud words: “Have we made thee a counsellor of the king? Forbear, why should they smite thee?” נתנּוּך is spoken collectively: We, the king, and the members of the council. And the prophet ceased, only answering the king thus: “I know that God hath determined to destroy thee, because thou hast done this (introduced Edomite idols), and hast not hearkened unto my counsel.” The prophet calls his warning “counsel,” referring to the king’s word, that he was not appointed a counsellor to the king.
entries.9f07df88461099325d82d0a9589f6827d907fd99: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.17-2Chr.25.24">2Ch 25:17-24</reference> <hi type="italic">The war with Joash, king of Israel</hi>. - Instead of following the counsel of the prophet, Amaziah consulted (sc., with his public officials or courtiers), and challenged King Joash of Israel to war. The challenge, and the war which followed, are also narrated in 2Ki 14:8-14 in agreement with our account, and have been already commented upon at that place, where we have also considered the occasion of this war, so fatal to Amaziah and the kingdom of Judah, on account of which has been handed down to us only in the supplementary narrative of the Chronicle. לך in <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.17">2Ch 25:17</reference> for לכה, come, as in Num 23:13 and Jdg 19:13. - In <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.20">2Ch 25:20</reference> the chronicler explains Amaziah’s refusal to hear the warning of Joash before the war with him, by a reference to the divine determination: “For it (came) of God (that Amaziah still went to war), that He might deliver them (the men of Judah) into the hand, because they had sought the gods of Edom.” בּיד נתן, to give into the power of the enemy. - In <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.23">2Ch 25:23</reference>, הפּונה שׁער is a manifest error for הפּנּה (2Ki 14:13). Were הפּונה, the gate that turns itself, faces (in some direction), correct, the direction would have to be given towards which it turned, e.g., Eze 8:3. - וגו וכל־הזּהב, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.24">2Ch 25:24</reference>, still depends upon תּפשׂ, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.23">2Ch 25:23</reference> : and (took away) all the gold, etc. In 2Ki 14:14, ולקח is supplied.<hi type="italic">The end of Amaziah’s reign;</hi> cf. 2Ki 14:17-20. - Although conquered and taken prisoner by Joash, Amaziah did not lose the throne. For Joash, contented with the carrying away of the treasures of the temple and of the palace, and the taking of hostages, set him again at liberty, so that he continued to reign, and outlived Joash by about fifteen years.
entries.60c1003808f1868815213b2e20a156825e775dd6: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.26">2Ch 25:26</reference> <div eID="gen6115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6116" type="x-p"/> On the book of the kings of Judah and Israel, see the Introduction.
entries.9b3c873e543b62d7171986357029660ca4d84aac: <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.27-2Chr.25.28">2Ch 25:27-28</reference> <div eID="gen6116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6117" type="x-p"/> On the conspiracy against Amaziah, his death, etc., see the commentary on 2Ki 14:17. יהוּדה בּעיר, in the city of Judah, is surprising, since everywhere else “the city of David” is mentioned as the burial-place, and even in our passage all the ancient versions have “in the city of David.” יהוּדה would therefore seem to be an orthographical error for דויד, occasioned by the immediately following יהוּדה.  <chapter eID="2Chr.25"/> <div eID="gen6117" type="x-p"/>
